newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sees lower tea production, exports in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees lower tea production, exports in 1997.

text.p: Kenyan tea production and exports reached a new high last year, but drought and poor global prices will undermine further gains in 1997, leading commercial farmers' agency and financial officials said on Thursday.
The Kenya Tea Growers Association (KTGA) put 1996 production at 257 million kg and exports at 244 million.
Output was far higher than the 246 million kg the KTGA forecast earlier and compared with 244 million in 1995. It did not give figures for 1995 exports.
Rains have just arrived in most growing areas, but too late to reverse a declining crop for this year.
"The drought has caused damage to tea bushes in the main growing districts and this will lead to a significant drop in production figures in 1997," KTGA chairman Musa Sang said.
And following the record 1996 crop, demand had not proved sufficient to support prices, he said.
"The prices fell steadily during the year and in the second half of 1996 producers sold their tea below cost of production," he added in the statement delivered at a KTGA gathering.
Sang said a strong shilling had adversely affected producers and exporting firms and saw a rate of 60-65 against the dollar as one that would be more suitable for exporters.
The shilling was quoted at a mean rate of 54.70 against the dollar on Thursday.
A senior central bank (CBK) official told KTGA members the bank welcomed a weaker shilling.

"The central bank would welcome an exchange rate depreciation to address some of the tea exporters problems, provided depreciation is supported with changes in economic fundamentals including inflation and balance of payments," CBK deputy governor Nzioki Kibua told the gathering.
Sang said tea companies also faced cash-flow problems because the government owed them 215 million shillings in value added tax refunds.
The refund is provided as a government tax incentive for commodity exporters. But exporters in most areas say it takes years to secure a refund.
Sang said delayed refunds reduced growers' ability to re-invest and develop estates.
The central bank's Kibua urged the tea sector to add value to exports through better packaging and processing, and to seek to improve quality by applying new technology.

Kibua said that maximum efforts should be made to open up new markets in the Middle East, Southeast Asia and the Far East. He urged the industry to take advantage of duty concessions offered in North America and the European Union to increase exports.
